name: Aekyom
confidence_why: The only account of Aekyom stress is Suter and Usher's 2017 second-hand summary of Stewart's unpublished 1989 SIL write-up, which reports that the language is tonal and that stressed syllables begin with aspirated stops but gives no placement rule and calls the suprasegmental phonology undescribed, while Voorhoeve 1975 notes only tentative contrastive pitch, so no stress system can be stated.
catalog_citation: Suter, Edgar & Timothy Usher. 2017. The Kamula-Elevala Language Family. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 35: 106-131 (secondary; reports Stewart, Jean. 1989. Aekyom language write-up, SIL ms, unreachable).
catalog_locator: p.109 (sec. 1.3, Aekyom phonology after Tables 2-3); p.116 (sec. 2.3); pp.119-120 (first-syllable vowel loss, ex. 5a-h)
catalog_quote: In her language write-up, Stewart (1989: 7ff) even distinguishes between heavily and lightly aspirated stops, but her description is phonetic and does not include a phonological analysis. Her account suggests that aspiration is found in the onset of stressed syllables and lack of aspiration goes along with a lack of stress. The aspirated and the unaspirated voiceless stop series are therefore probably allophones of one phonological stop series. ... Neither is tone marked in the orthography, although the language is tonal (Stewart 1989: 22f). ... We know that all three languages are tonal, but as tone is not rendered in the orthography we have been unable to incorporate it into our reconstructions. The role stress played in the history of the Kamula-Elevala languages is not well understood, either. To arrive at a better understanding of the comparative phonology, a good description of th…

Glottolog's descriptive bibliography has only that one ms; Voorhoeve 1975 (held, pp.389-390) adds only 'some evidence.. contrastive pitch' and is silent on stress. nothing found suggests a published phonology, JIPA illustration, thesis or instrumental study of Aek

sources.note: The only primary description of Aekyom phonetics; our not determinable code rests on Suter & Usher's two-sentence paraphrase of its pp.7ff (aspiration tied to stressed syllables) and 22f (tone). Reading it directly would settle whether Stewart states any stress-placement tendency or describes the tone system, and could move the record to a positive code or to tonal.

sources.note: Marks three stop series (p' t' k' vs p t k) which Suter & Usher interpret as stress-conditioned aspiration; the dictionary's front matter/orthography notes and the distribution of aspirated stops across ~all entries would show where stressed syllables fall (e.g. whether aspiration is word-initial only), a cheap empirical check on any placement tendency.
